developmentalQuestion: How do historians decide which explanation is stronger?
studentReasoningIntro: More than one interpretation can contain part of the truth. Historians compare what each explanation claims, what evidence it accounts for, what evidence creates trouble, and whether a qualification would make it stronger.
reasoningReviewPrompts: What is each interpretation actually claiming?
What evidence does each explanation account for?
What evidence complicates or weakens it?
Which interpretation has greater explanatory power?
Could the weaker interpretation still explain part of the story?
What qualification would improve the argument?

When Does Opposition Become Treason?
lectureTitles.core: Faction, repression, loyal opposition, and transfer of power

lectureTitles.title: Can a Republic Have an Empire?
lectureTitles.core: Expansion, constitutional power, claim, and sovereignty

lectureTitles.title: Why Did a Republic That Feared War Choose War?
lectureTitles.core: Maritime sovereignty, failed alternatives, Indigenous agency, converging crises, and a divided decision

questions.stem: Which interpretation best explains how the Constitution became a functioning national government after 1789?

choices.text: The Constitution itself supplied enough detail that later officials mainly had to follow written instructions.
choices.feedback: The Constitution mattered, but the lecture emphasizes how many operating routines were not specified and had to be created in practice.

choices.text: Washington's personal popularity was the main reason the new government could function.
choices.feedback: Washington's reputation helped, but popularity alone does not explain Cabinet practice, treaty consultation, public credit, or enforcement.

choices.text: Written powers became workable through precedents, administrative routines, and new fiscal capacity.
choices.feedback: This interpretation explains both the missing operating rules and the government's growing ability to act.

choices.text: Hamilton's financial program alone transformed the Constitution into a working government.
choices.feedback: Hamilton's program was central to capacity, but it does not explain the institutional precedents created by Washington and the First Congress.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. The strongest explanation joins constitutional text to practice: precedents made institutions workable, while fiscal capacity made federal power effective.
questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. Ask which interpretation explains both the institutional problem and the government's growing capacity to act.
walkthrough: Identify the outcome: a written Constitution became an operating government.
Test each interpretation against more than one part of the lecture.
Washington's popularity explains legitimacy, and Hamilton explains fiscal capacity, but each covers only part of the evidence.
The precedent-and-capacity interpretation explains the Senate experiment, Cabinet development, finance, taxation, and enforcement together.
The weaker explanations are partial, not useless. They simply explain less of the evidence.
questions.transferStrategy: For competing explanations, prefer the interpretation that accounts for the most evidence without pretending the smaller explanations are completely false.
questions.hint: Which answer can explain both Washington's institutional experiments and Hamilton's state-building?

sourceAlignment.primarySource: Chapter 7 final formal lecture decks and Chapter 7 Historian's Notebook
sourceAlignment.lectureClaim: The Constitution became real through precedent and capacity, not text alone.
sourceAlignment.notes: Practice-only item. Optional Rabbit Hole / Want to Go Deeper material is excluded.

questions.accessibilityNotes: Text-only item. No image is required.

reasoningReview.partialValidity: Washington's reputation helps explain legitimacy, while Hamilton's program explains fiscal capacity. Each is useful but too narrow by itself.
reasoningReview.qualification: Precedent and capacity made the government workable, but public legitimacy also shaped whether people accepted its new routines and powers.

questions.stem: Which interpretation gives the Whiskey Rebellion the greatest explanatory importance?

choices.text: It was mainly a dispute over whether western farmers liked paying taxes.
choices.feedback: Tax burden mattered, but this interpretation is too narrow to explain why the federal government mobilized overwhelming force.

choices.text: It tested whether a constitutional republic could enforce a law while still claiming to protect liberty.
choices.feedback: This captures the lecture's central tension between state capacity and republican legitimacy.

choices.text: It proved that the new federal government intended to punish all political dissent by force.
choices.feedback: The mobilization was coercive, but the absence of a major battle and the later pardons complicate this interpretation.

choices.text: It showed that the Constitution had failed because resistance continued after ratification.
choices.feedback: The episode showed conflict over legitimacy, not constitutional collapse.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. The rebellion mattered because it tested whether enforcement under an elected constitutional government would be seen as legitimate rather than tyrannical.
questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. Look for the interpretation that explains both federal enforcement and the continuing argument about liberty.
walkthrough: Start with the event: resistance to the whiskey excise became armed enough to trigger federal mobilization.
Ask what larger problem the event revealed, not merely what the protesters disliked.
Federalists saw proof that laws could be enforced; Republicans could see dangerous coercive capacity.
The best interpretation explains why the same event could support both conclusions.
The narrow tax interpretation remains part of the story, but it does not explain the constitutional stakes.
questions.transferStrategy: When judging significance, ask what larger historical problem an event exposed or tested.
questions.hint: What makes the event more than a tax protest?

sourceAlignment.primarySource: Chapter 7 final formal lecture decks and Chapter 7 Historian's Notebook
sourceAlignment.lectureClaim: The Whiskey Rebellion tested whether federal power could be both effective and legitimate.
sourceAlignment.notes: Practice-only item. Optional Rabbit Hole / Want to Go Deeper material is excluded.

questions.accessibilityNotes: Text-only item. No image is required.

reasoningReview.partialValidity: The tax burden and western farmers' local economy help explain why resistance began, even though they do not explain the episode's full constitutional importance.
reasoningReview.qualification: The rebellion demonstrated federal capacity, but the lack of a major battle and the pardons qualify a simple story of unchecked coercion.

questions.stem: Which explanation best captures why the Bank debate mattered beyond banking?

choices.text: It forced Americans to decide whether legitimate constitutional ends could justify powers not listed word-for-word.
choices.feedback: This interpretation explains why the debate became a test of how the Constitution would operate in practice.

choices.text: It showed that Jefferson and Hamilton disagreed mainly because they represented different occupations.
choices.feedback: Social interests mattered, but the lecture uses the Bank debate primarily to expose a constitutional disagreement.

choices.text: It settled the meaning of every federal power for the rest of American history.
choices.feedback: The debate created a precedent, but it did not permanently settle every constitutional dispute.

choices.text: It was mostly a technical disagreement over whether paper money was useful.
choices.feedback: That is too narrow. The central issue was the scope of implied federal power.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. The Bank controversy made constitutional interpretation itself part of governing: how broadly could the national government choose means to carry out legitimate ends?
questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. Ask what constitutional problem the Bank debate exposed.
walkthrough: Identify the immediate topic: a national bank.
Now separate the policy from the constitutional question underneath it.
Jefferson feared that broad implied power could erase limits; Hamilton argued that legitimate ends required useful means.
The stronger interpretation explains both arguments and why the dispute mattered beyond finance.
A technical banking interpretation explains the setting but not the historical significance.
questions.transferStrategy: Move from the policy dispute to the constitutional principle that made the dispute important.
questions.hint: What did Jefferson and Hamilton disagree about besides the usefulness of a bank?

sourceAlignment.primarySource: Chapter 7 final formal lecture decks and Chapter 7 Historian's Notebook
sourceAlignment.lectureClaim: The Bank debate showed how constitutional meaning developed through arguments about implied powers.
sourceAlignment.notes: Practice-only item. Optional Rabbit Hole / Want to Go Deeper material is excluded.

questions.accessibilityNotes: Text-only item. No image is required.

reasoningReview.partialValidity: Banking policy and competing economic interests mattered, but they do not fully explain why the dispute became a lasting constitutional argument.
reasoningReview.qualification: The debate centered on implied power while also carrying real disagreements about finance, interests, and the risks of concentrated authority.

questions.stem: Why did organized political opposition appear dangerous to many Americans in the 1790s?

choices.text: Because Americans had already accepted modern political parties and feared they were becoming too competitive.
choices.feedback: The problem was almost the reverse: organized parties were not yet accepted as a normal part of republican government.

choices.text: Because the Constitution explicitly prohibited political parties and treated organized opposition as illegal.
choices.feedback: The Constitution did not ban parties. The fear came from republican political culture and crisis, not a constitutional prohibition.

choices.text: Because every opposition newspaper openly supported a foreign invasion of the United States.
choices.feedback: Partisan newspapers could be fierce, but this overstates the evidence and collapses criticism into treason.

choices.text: Because opposition looked like faction, and foreign crises made domestic critics easier to imagine as disloyal.
choices.feedback: This combines the older fear of faction with the new pressure created by France, Genêt, XYZ, and the Quasi-War.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. Opposition became frightening because older fears of faction collided with foreign crisis, making partisan critics look potentially disloyal.
questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. Look for an explanation that combines political culture with the pressure of international crisis.
walkthrough: Begin with the political context: many Americans associated organized faction with selfish attacks on the common good.
Add the foreign-policy context: the French Revolution, Genêt, XYZ, and naval conflict made loyalty feel urgent.
Ask which explanation can account for both the fear of parties and the escalation of repression.
The combined interpretation has greater explanatory power than either factional fear or foreign crisis alone.
That does not prove repression was justified; it explains why it became politically plausible.
questions.transferStrategy: For context, combine the political assumptions people already held with the crisis that made those assumptions more powerful.
questions.hint: Which answer explains why opposition seemed especially dangerous at that particular moment?

sourceAlignment.primarySource: Chapter 7 final formal lecture decks and Chapter 7 Historian's Notebook
sourceAlignment.lectureClaim: Foreign crisis intensified an existing fear that organized faction could endanger the republic.
sourceAlignment.notes: Practice-only item. Optional Rabbit Hole / Want to Go Deeper material is excluded.

questions.accessibilityNotes: Text-only item. No image is required.

reasoningReview.partialValidity: Foreign danger was real, so security concerns were not invented. That still does not make every domestic critic disloyal.
reasoningReview.qualification: Foreign crisis intensified an older fear of faction; it made repression plausible without proving that repression was justified.

questions.stem: Which interpretation best explains the historical importance of Matthew Lyon winning reelection from jail?

choices.text: It proved that the Sedition Act had ended organized Republican politics.
choices.feedback: His reelection shows the opposite: voters could continue supporting an opposition politician even after federal prosecution.

choices.text: It showed a collision between federal repression and voters' claim to choose their own representative.
choices.feedback: This captures why Lyon makes the Sedition crisis concrete rather than abstract.

choices.text: It demonstrated that voters across the entire country unanimously opposed the Sedition Act.
choices.feedback: His victory is evidence of political resistance, but it does not show unanimous public opinion.

choices.text: It mattered mainly because jail automatically made candidates more popular.
choices.feedback: The significance lies in the conflict over legitimate opposition, not a general rule about jailed candidates.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. Lyon's reelection showed that federal prosecution could not automatically erase the political legitimacy voters gave an opposition candidate.
questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. Ask what two kinds of authority collided in Lyon's story.
walkthrough: Identify the two facts that matter together: federal conviction and electoral victory.
Ask what each fact represents: government repression on one side, voter choice on the other.
The strongest interpretation explains the contradiction between those two forms of authority.
That contradiction helps explain why the Sedition Act became a test of legitimate opposition.
A claim about universal public opinion goes beyond the evidence.
questions.transferStrategy: When a single person's story matters, ask what larger institutions or principles collide inside that story.
questions.hint: Why does reelection matter more than the jail sentence by itself?

sourceAlignment.primarySource: Chapter 7 final formal lecture decks and Chapter 7 Historian's Notebook
sourceAlignment.lectureClaim: Matthew Lyon makes the conflict between repression and electoral legitimacy visible.
sourceAlignment.notes: Practice-only item. Optional Rabbit Hole / Want to Go Deeper material is excluded.

questions.accessibilityNotes: Text-only item. No image is required.

reasoningReview.partialValidity: Federal prosecution shows the reach of repression, while Lyon's victory shows the continuing force of electoral legitimacy.
reasoningReview.qualification: Lyon's reelection demonstrates resistance within his constituency, not unanimous public opposition to the Sedition Act.

questions.stem: Which explanation best accounts for why the election and transfer of power in 1800–1801 became a constitutional precedent?

choices.text: The election ended party conflict because both sides accepted a lasting national consensus.
choices.feedback: Partisan conflict continued. The precedent was not the disappearance of parties.

choices.text: The victorious party rewrote the Constitution before it allowed the transfer of executive power.
choices.feedback: No constitutional rewrite created the central precedent discussed in lecture.

choices.text: A bitter contest ended with the losing party yielding office while the winning opposition stayed inside the constitutional system.
choices.feedback: This explains why loser’s consent became the central lesson of the transfer.

choices.text: The election proved that political conflict no longer threatened republican government.
choices.feedback: The transfer showed that conflict could be survived; it did not eliminate danger or disagreement.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. The crucial precedent was that losing office did not require overthrowing the system or outlawing the opposition.
questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. Focus on what the defeated party actually did after a deeply partisan election.
walkthrough: Start with the problem: each side feared the other could destroy the republic.
Then identify the outcome: power changed hands through constitutional procedures.
Ask what new expectation that outcome created.
The strongest explanation is not that conflict disappeared, but that constitutional government survived partisan defeat.
That is why the transfer matters as a precedent for loyal opposition.
questions.transferStrategy: For political transitions, distinguish 'conflict disappeared' from 'institutions survived conflict.'
questions.hint: What changed even though partisan hostility did not disappear?

sourceAlignment.primarySource: Chapter 7 final formal lecture decks and Chapter 7 Historian's Notebook
sourceAlignment.lectureClaim: The 1801 transfer helped normalize the idea that an opposition party could become the government without ending the republic.
sourceAlignment.notes: Practice-only item. Optional Rabbit Hole / Want to Go Deeper material is excluded.

questions.accessibilityNotes: Text-only item. No image is required.

reasoningReview.partialValidity: Jefferson's victory mattered, but the stronger explanation centers on the losing party yielding power while remaining a legal opposition.
reasoningReview.qualification: The transfer normalized partisan succession without ending party conflict or removing the constitutional system's inequalities.

questions.stem: Which interpretation best explains why Jefferson accepted the Louisiana Purchase despite his concern about limited federal power?

choices.text: The strategic value and fleeting nature of the opportunity outweighed his desire for a narrow reading of federal power.
choices.feedback: This captures the tension between principle and governing contingency.

choices.text: Jefferson abandoned all constitutional principles as soon as he became president.
choices.feedback: The lecture treats his dilemma as genuine. He worried about constitutional authority even while accepting the opportunity.

choices.text: The Constitution clearly and specifically authorized the president to purchase foreign territory.
choices.feedback: The lecture emphasizes the opposite: the constitutional authority was not neatly stated.

choices.text: Jefferson cared only about increasing presidential power and not about western security.
choices.feedback: This misses the New Orleans crisis and the strategic logic of the purchase.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. Jefferson's decision shows how governing contingency could push a limited-government president toward broader practical power.
questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. Look for the interpretation that explains both his constitutional hesitation and his decision to act.
walkthrough: Identify Jefferson's principle: federal power should remain limited to delegated authority.
Identify the strategic problem: New Orleans and the Mississippi affected western security and national unity.
Add contingency: France unexpectedly offered all Louisiana, and the opportunity might disappear.
The strongest interpretation explains why principle and circumstance pulled in different directions.
Calling this simple hypocrisy names the contradiction but does not explain the decision.
questions.transferStrategy: When an actor seems inconsistent, test whether changing circumstances created a genuine tradeoff between principles.
questions.hint: Which answer explains both the hesitation and the action?

sourceAlignment.primarySource: Chapter 7 final formal lecture decks and Chapter 7 Historian's Notebook
sourceAlignment.lectureClaim: Jefferson's Purchase decision joined limited-government principle to strategic contingency.
sourceAlignment.notes: Practice-only item. Optional Rabbit Hole / Want to Go Deeper material is excluded.

questions.accessibilityNotes: Text-only item. No image is required.

reasoningReview.partialValidity: Jefferson's limited-government principles were genuine, and the strategic opportunity was unusually valuable. The decision grew from the collision between them.
reasoningReview.qualification: Contingency explains why Jefferson acted broadly, but it does not erase the constitutional tension he recognized.

questions.stem: Which interpretation best explains the lecture's warning that the Louisiana Purchase map can be misleading?

choices.text: The map is useless because the United States acquired nothing meaningful in 1803.
choices.feedback: The treaty mattered greatly. The problem is not that the map is useless, but that its colored borders can imply more control than existed.

choices.text: The map is misleading only because cartographers had not yet discovered the Mississippi River.
choices.feedback: The lecture's concern is sovereignty, not basic ignorance of the Mississippi.

choices.text: The map proves that Native nations immediately accepted United States authority after the purchase.
choices.feedback: This reverses the lecture's argument about continuing Native sovereignty.

choices.text: The treaty transferred a U.S. claim, but Native nations still exercised power over homelands, trade, and diplomacy on the ground.
choices.feedback: This directly explains the difference between a legal claim and effective sovereignty.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. The map records a change in imperial claim, not the instant disappearance of Native sovereignty or the arrival of effective U.S. control everywhere.
questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. Ask what a colored territorial claim can show and what it cannot show.
walkthrough: Identify what the map represents: a legal and diplomatic claim transferred from France to the United States.
Identify what the map cannot automatically represent: consent, effective administration, or control on the ground.
Use the Lakota confrontation and the expedition's dependence on Native communities as tests.
The strongest interpretation explains both the map's usefulness and its limits.
Historians do not reject the map; they interpret what kind of evidence it is.
questions.transferStrategy: For maps, ask what the boundaries represent: claim, control, population, sovereignty, or something else.
questions.hint: What did Native nations still control after the treaty was signed?

sourceAlignment.primarySource: Chapter 7 final formal lecture decks and Chapter 7 Historian's Notebook
sourceAlignment.lectureClaim: The Louisiana map records a claim more clearly than it records effective sovereignty.
sourceAlignment.notes: Practice-only item. Optional Rabbit Hole / Want to Go Deeper material is excluded.

questions.accessibilityNotes: Text-only item. No image is required.

reasoningReview.partialValidity: The map accurately records a transferred imperial claim; it becomes misleading only when claim is mistaken for control or consent.
reasoningReview.qualification: The Purchase expanded U.S. claims quickly, while effective sovereignty still depended on diplomacy, knowledge, and power on the ground.

questions.stem: Which interpretation best explains why war with Britain became thinkable by 1812?

choices.text: The desire among some War Hawks to take Canada became the single motive that caused the war.
choices.feedback: Expansion toward Canada mattered to some politicians, but this explanation does not account for impressment, Chesapeake, failed coercion, or the western crisis.

choices.text: Republicans had always wanted a large war because war strengthened the federal government.
choices.feedback: The lecture begins with the opposite problem: Republicans feared the armies, debt, taxes, and state expansion war could create.

choices.text: Maritime pressure, failed alternatives, and western conflict increasingly appeared as one sovereignty crisis.
choices.feedback: This interpretation explains the largest range of evidence while preserving the role of multiple causes.

choices.text: The United States entered the war only after Britain invaded and burned Washington, D.C.
choices.feedback: That event occurred after the declaration of war and cannot explain the 1812 decision.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. War became thinkable as several pressures converged and nonwar alternatives seemed less capable of defending sovereignty.
questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. Look for the explanation that can account for the maritime crisis, the western crisis, and the failure of alternatives together.
walkthrough: List the evidence the explanation must cover: impressment, Chesapeake, embargo, later alternatives, Tecumseh and Tenskwatawa, Tippecanoe, War Hawks, and the war message.
Test the single-cause interpretation. Canada explains part of the politics but not the whole chain.
Test the claim that Republicans wanted war all along. It conflicts with years of attempted alternatives.
The convergence interpretation explains more evidence with fewer exceptions.
The weaker explanations can still be partial contributors without becoming the main explanation.
questions.transferStrategy: For multi-causal events, test whether one explanation can account for evidence from different arenas, not just the most memorable cause.
questions.hint: Which explanation can survive evidence from both the Atlantic and the West?

sourceAlignment.primarySource: Chapter 7 final formal lecture decks and Chapter 7 Historian's Notebook
sourceAlignment.lectureClaim: The lecture presents the road to war as a convergence of maritime, western, and policy failures.
sourceAlignment.notes: Practice-only item. Optional Rabbit Hole / Want to Go Deeper material is excluded.

questions.accessibilityNotes: Text-only item. No image is required.

reasoningReview.partialValidity: Impressment, War Hawk advocacy, Canada, and western conflict each explain part of the road to war, but no single factor explains the timing as well.
reasoningReview.qualification: War became thinkable through converging crises and failed alternatives, yet Congress's divided vote shows it never became an uncontested choice.

questions.stem: What does the divided congressional vote for war most strongly add to our interpretation of 1812?

choices.text: It proves that almost no Americans considered British maritime policy or impressment a serious national problem.
choices.feedback: Opposition to war did not mean indifference to impressment or maritime pressure.

choices.text: It shows that Americans agreed on British wrongdoing but disagreed sharply over whether war was the right response.
choices.feedback: This matches the lecture's point that grievance and policy choice were not the same thing.

choices.text: It shows that War Hawks had no influence on Congress or on the final decision to declare war.
choices.feedback: War Hawks mattered, but influence is different from unanimous control.

choices.text: It proves that the causes of war were imaginary because the vote was not unanimous.
choices.feedback: Political division does not make the underlying grievances unreal.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. The vote complicates the phrase 'America chose war' by showing that a divided republic debated whether real grievances justified this particular response.
questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. Use the vote to distinguish agreement about a problem from agreement about a policy.
walkthrough: Identify what the vote can tell us: Congress was deeply divided.
Do not infer that opposition to war means opposition to every grievance.
Compare the evidence of British pressure with the evidence of political disagreement.
The strongest interpretation preserves both: the grievances were real, and the decision for war was contested.
This is a useful example of evidence qualifying an argument rather than simply overturning it.
questions.transferStrategy: When new evidence complicates a broad statement, revise the statement rather than throwing it away.
questions.hint: What distinction can we make between recognizing a grievance and choosing a response?

sourceAlignment.primarySource: Chapter 7 final formal lecture decks and Chapter 7 Historian's Notebook
sourceAlignment.lectureClaim: The vote qualifies 'America chose war' into 'a divided republic chose war.'
sourceAlignment.notes: Practice-only item. Optional Rabbit Hole / Want to Go Deeper material is excluded.

questions.accessibilityNotes: Text-only item. No image is required.

reasoningReview.partialValidity: British violations help explain support for war, but they do not explain why many representatives rejected war as the remedy.
reasoningReview.qualification: A divided republic chose war: national policy followed constitutional voting, not public unanimity.

questions.stem: Which interpretation best explains why Hamilton treated public credit as a problem of national power?

choices.text: Paying creditors would make every dispute over federal policy disappear.
choices.feedback: Credit could strengthen capacity, but it could not eliminate political conflict.

choices.text: Assumption mattered only because states had no remaining debts of their own.
choices.feedback: States differed, and assumption shifted obligations and political gravity toward the federal government.

choices.text: Public credit was mainly a symbolic effort to make Hamilton personally popular.
choices.feedback: The lecture emphasizes institutional credibility and capacity, not Hamilton's popularity.

choices.text: Reliable repayment would let the government borrow, survive crises, and make national commitments credible.
choices.feedback: This connects debt repayment to the government's practical ability to act.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. Hamilton linked repayment to the capacity to borrow, respond to crisis, and make federal promises credible.
questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. Ask what a government gains when lenders believe it will honor its obligations.
walkthrough: Identify Hamilton's immediate problem: the government had debts and uncertain credit.
Ask what reliable repayment would make possible later, especially during crisis or war.
The strongest interpretation connects credibility to borrowing and state capacity rather than to popularity alone.
That explanation can still be qualified by asking who benefited and who carried the costs.
questions.transferStrategy: For institutional causes, trace how a policy changes what a government can do, not only who supports it.
questions.hint: What becomes possible when creditors trust a government?

sourceAlignment.primarySource: Chapter 7 Lecture 1 and Chapter 7 Historian's Notebook
sourceAlignment.lectureClaim: Hamilton treated public credit as the foundation of borrowing capacity and national credibility.
sourceAlignment.notes: Formal instructional stream only; optional enrichment excluded. Practice-only wording.

questions.accessibilityNotes: Text-only item; no image or outside source is required.

reasoningReview.partialValidity: The program affected interests and political loyalties, but those effects do not replace Hamilton's central capacity argument.
reasoningReview.qualification: Public credit strengthened national capacity while also creating distributive and political conflicts that the capacity explanation should not erase.

questions.stem: Which explanation best accounts for newspapers becoming central to organized opposition in the 1790s?

choices.text: Newspapers helped turn criticism into a shared public campaign that could organize meetings, petitions, and electoral opposition.
choices.feedback: This explains how print became political infrastructure, not just a source of information.

choices.text: Newspapers created every disagreement before leaders had any policy conflicts.
choices.feedback: Newspapers organized conflict, but they did not invent all of its political causes.

choices.text: Printers replaced elections, making voting unnecessary for political organization.
choices.feedback: Partisan print worked with elections, meetings, and petitions rather than replacing them.

choices.text: The Constitution required each emerging party to publish an official newspaper.
choices.feedback: No constitutional rule created party newspapers; they developed through political practice.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. Partisan newspapers helped transform disagreement into organized, public, and sustained opposition.
questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. Focus on how print connected individual criticism to collective political action.
walkthrough: Separate the existence of disagreement from the means used to organize it.
Newspapers circulated arguments, identified allies, and linked readers to meetings, petitions, and elections.
The infrastructure explanation accounts for political coordination without claiming that print invented every conflict.
Foreign crisis later made this organized opposition appear more threatening.
questions.transferStrategy: When explaining political organization, identify the institutions that turn private views into coordinated public action.
questions.hint: What could a newspaper do beyond reporting that a disagreement existed?

sourceAlignment.primarySource: Chapter 7 Lecture 2 and Chapter 7 Historian's Notebook
sourceAlignment.lectureClaim: Partisan newspapers helped create and organize political opposition through public communication.
sourceAlignment.notes: Formal instructional stream only; optional enrichment excluded. Practice-only wording.

questions.accessibilityNotes: Text-only item; no image or outside source is required.

reasoningReview.partialValidity: Policy disputes and personal rivalries existed before the press organized them, so newspapers were an enabling cause rather than the sole origin of partisanship.
reasoningReview.qualification: Print helped build party organization while elections, meetings, petitions, and foreign crisis also shaped the emerging opposition.

questions.stem: Which explanation gives events in Saint-Domingue the right weight in the Louisiana Purchase?

choices.text: Events in Saint-Domingue played no part in changing France's strategic calculation about Louisiana.
choices.feedback: The failure of the Caribbean project changed Louisiana's strategic usefulness to France.

choices.text: The Haitian Revolution alone completed the Purchase without French or American decisions.
choices.feedback: It changed the opportunity, but Napoleon, the envoys, and Jefferson still made consequential choices.

choices.text: The collapse of Napoleon's Caribbean project reduced Louisiana's value, helping make a sale possible with other pressures.
choices.feedback: This treats Saint-Domingue as a major contingent cause without turning it into the only cause.

choices.text: France offered Louisiana because it had already established secure control across North America.
choices.feedback: Louisiana had become harder to use and defend, not securely controlled as a continental empire.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. Resistance and disease helped wreck Napoleon's Caribbean plan, changing Louisiana's value without mechanically causing the sale by themselves.
questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. Give Saint-Domingue real causal weight without treating it as the only decision in the story.
walkthrough: Identify France's larger plan: rebuild a Caribbean slave empire supported by Louisiana.
Resistance and epidemic disease devastated that project and made Louisiana less useful and harder to defend.
The strongest explanation then adds Napoleon's strategy, the New Orleans crisis, and the envoys' decision.
This is contingency: an outcome in one region changed the choices available in another.
questions.transferStrategy: For multicausal explanation, give a major turning point real weight while still naming the decisions and conditions that connected it to the outcome.
questions.hint: Did Saint-Domingue make the sale automatic, or did it change the strategic opportunity?

sourceAlignment.primarySource: Chapter 7 Lecture 3 and Chapter 7 Historian's Notebook
sourceAlignment.lectureClaim: The collapse of Napoleon's Caribbean project helped make Louisiana available but did not alone cause the Purchase.
sourceAlignment.notes: Formal instructional stream only; optional enrichment excluded. Practice-only wording.

questions.accessibilityNotes: Text-only item; no image or outside source is required.

reasoningReview.partialValidity: Napoleon's choices and the U.S. need for New Orleans remain essential, but neither explains why France's strategic calculation changed when it did.
reasoningReview.qualification: Saint-Domingue helped make the sale possible; French strategy, American urgency, and diplomatic choice turned that possibility into the Purchase.

questions.stem: Which interpretation best explains why the Lewis and Clark expedition both expanded U.S. power and revealed its limits?

choices.text: It proved the United States already governed every community within the purchased claim.
choices.feedback: Repeated dependence on Native diplomacy and knowledge contradicts complete control.

choices.text: It gathered knowledge and announced U.S. claims, while dependence on Native communities exposed incomplete sovereignty.
choices.feedback: This interpretation accounts for both the expedition's state-building purpose and its practical limits.

choices.text: It had no political purpose because it also collected scientific information.
choices.feedback: Scientific, commercial, diplomatic, and political goals operated together.

choices.text: It failed whenever expedition members accepted help from Native communities.
choices.feedback: Native assistance made the expedition possible; dependence reveals limits without turning the journey into simple failure.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. The expedition converted knowledge into state capacity, yet its dependence showed that U.S. claims were not the same as effective sovereignty.
questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. Choose the interpretation that can explain both what the expedition added and what its dependence revealed.
walkthrough: List what the expedition produced: maps, observations, diplomatic information, and a public U.S. claim.
Then list what it needed: Native trade, interpreters, horses, routes, and permission to move.
An interpretation of complete mastery explains the first list but fails the second.
The stronger interpretation holds expansion and limitation together.
questions.transferStrategy: When evidence points in two directions, build an interpretation that explains both instead of discarding the inconvenient half.
questions.hint: What interpretation can account for both state knowledge and Native assistance?

sourceAlignment.primarySource: Chapter 7 Lecture 3 and Chapter 7 Historian's Notebook
sourceAlignment.lectureClaim: Lewis and Clark extended U.S. knowledge and claims while depending on Native diplomatic and commercial worlds.
sourceAlignment.notes: Formal instructional stream only; optional enrichment excluded. Practice-only wording.

questions.accessibilityNotes: Text-only item; no image or outside source is required.

reasoningReview.partialValidity: The expedition did strengthen U.S. knowledge and diplomatic claims, so an expansion interpretation explains part of the evidence.
reasoningReview.qualification: It expanded state knowledge and claims without proving complete control; dependency is evidence of contested sovereignty, not of a purposeless expedition.

questions.stem: Which interpretation gives the War Hawks the strongest but properly qualified role in the decision for war?

choices.text: They invented every grievance and forced a united country into war for Canada alone.
choices.feedback: Maritime and western grievances predated their influence, and the vote was sharply divided.

choices.text: They mattered only after war began and therefore did not affect the congressional choice.
choices.feedback: Militant Republicans helped raise the political temperature before the declaration.

choices.text: They opposed attempts to connect British maritime pressure with western conflict and Native resistance.
choices.feedback: War advocates helped present those problems as parts of a larger sovereignty crisis.

choices.text: They made war politically possible by pressing existing grievances after alternatives failed, without causing the crisis alone.
choices.feedback: This gives political advocacy real weight while preserving the broader causal setting.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. War Hawks helped convert an existing, converging crisis into congressional action; they did not create every cause or a national consensus.
questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. Give political advocates real influence without treating them as the only source of the crisis.
walkthrough: Separate the grievances from the people who organized support for a policy response.
Impressment, failed alternatives, and western conflict already existed.
War Hawks gained institutional influence and helped frame war as the necessary answer.
The divided vote shows their success was consequential but incomplete.
questions.transferStrategy: Distinguish people who make an outcome politically possible from the deeper conditions that created the problem they mobilized around.
questions.hint: Did the War Hawks create the crisis, or did they help turn it into a policy choice?

questions.stem: A historian claims the Constitution's text fully designed the early presidency. New evidence shows Washington abandoned unworkable Senate consultation and began relying on department heads. How should the claim change?

choices.text: It complicates the claim by showing that practice and precedent helped determine how the presidency actually worked.
choices.feedback: This is the best use of the evidence: it does not deny the Constitution mattered, but it shows text alone was insufficient.

choices.text: It strongly supports the claim because experimentation proves the written design was complete.
choices.feedback: Experimentation points to gaps in the operating routine, not a fully specified design.

choices.text: It proves the Constitution had no influence on presidential government at all.
choices.feedback: That goes too far. Washington was acting within constitutional offices and powers even while working out procedures.

choices.text: It is irrelevant because Senate consultation has nothing to do with executive practice.
choices.feedback: The episode directly concerns how the executive and Senate would use the Constitution's advice-and-consent language.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. The evidence does not erase the constitutional text; it qualifies the claim by showing that operating rules emerged through practice.
questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. Ask whether the evidence supports text alone, rejects text entirely, or requires a more qualified interpretation.
walkthrough: State the original claim precisely: the text had already designed how the presidency would operate.
Identify the new evidence: Washington experimented and changed his procedure after the first approach failed.
Ask whether that evidence fits a fully specified operating design.
It does not. But the Constitution still supplied the offices and powers, so the strongest conclusion is 'complicate,' not 'destroy.'
A better interpretation would say constitutional text and precedent worked together.
questions.transferStrategy: When testing a claim, avoid all-or-nothing choices. Evidence often requires qualification rather than total rejection.
questions.hint: Does the new evidence make the Constitution irrelevant, or does it show the text needed practice?

questions.stem: A historian claims, 'The Whiskey Rebellion proves the new federal government was simply becoming tyrannical.' Which additional evidence from the lecture most strongly complicates that interpretation?

choices.text: The government demonstrated coercive power by mobilizing a militia force of about 13,000.
choices.feedback: This supports the claim's coercive side more than it complicates it.

choices.text: The resistance began around a federal excise tax that burdened western producers.
choices.feedback: That explains the dispute but does not directly complicate the tyranny interpretation.

choices.text: The resistance dispersed without a major battle, and Washington pardoned the two men convicted of treason.
choices.feedback: This adds evidence of restraint after enforcement and therefore complicates a simple tyranny interpretation.

choices.text: Hamilton argued that reliable excise revenue was necessary to sustain public credit.
choices.feedback: That explains federal reasoning, but the strongest complication is evidence about how coercion actually ended.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. The force was real, but the ending matters: enforcement was followed by legal process and pardons rather than mass punishment.
questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. Look for evidence that directly changes how we interpret the government's use of force.
walkthrough: Identify the interpretation: federal enforcement equals simple tyranny.
Look for evidence that supports it: the large militia mobilization.
Now look for evidence that creates friction with it.
The lack of a major battle and later pardons show that coercive capacity and restraint existed together.
The best interpretation should therefore preserve the coercion without reducing the episode to coercion alone.
questions.transferStrategy: To complicate an argument, look for evidence that is hard for the argument to explain without qualification.
questions.hint: What happened after the militia was called out?

questions.stem: During an international crisis, a movement publishes harsh criticism of the government. A historian treats the criticism as disloyal by definition. Which Chapter 7 lesson best tests that claim?

choices.text: Foreign crises never create legitimate security concerns for a constitutional republic.
choices.feedback: XYZ and the Quasi-War show that real international danger existed.

choices.text: Any group criticizing an administration during a crisis automatically acts as loyal opposition.
choices.feedback: The lecture does not make loyalty automatic; it asks where the boundary should be drawn.

choices.text: The best test of loyalty is whether criticism appears in print rather than at a public meeting.
choices.feedback: The medium alone does not determine whether the action is legitimate opposition or treason.

choices.text: Foreign crisis can make opposition appear dangerous, but the 1790s show why a republic must distinguish criticism from treason.
choices.feedback: This applies the lecture's central lesson without pretending foreign danger was imaginary.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. The 1790s teach us to hold two facts together: foreign danger can be real, and opposition still requires room to remain legitimate.
questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. Apply the lecture's distinction between explaining why fear grew and justifying every act of repression.
walkthrough: Identify the new claim: emergency context automatically turns criticism into disloyalty.
Recall the lecture's evidence that Federalist fears were not invented.
Now recall the Sedition Act and Lyon: treating opposition as treason created a constitutional problem.
The strongest application preserves both security and opposition rather than making either absolute.
That is how historical context can explain a response without automatically endorsing it.
questions.transferStrategy: Separate 'this fear made sense in context' from 'therefore every response to the fear was justified.'
questions.hint: Does explaining Federalist fear require accepting the Sedition Act as necessary?

questions.stem: A new 1801 letter says, 'We lost the election, but we will organize to defeat the new administration rather than resist the transfer of office.' Which interpretation would it most strongly support?

choices.text: Political parties had disappeared after the election.
choices.feedback: The letter explicitly describes continued party organization.

choices.text: Loser's consent was becoming compatible with continued partisan opposition.
choices.feedback: The evidence directly joins acceptance of transfer with plans for future opposition.

choices.text: The losing side believed the new administration was unquestionably correct.
choices.feedback: Accepting constitutional defeat does not imply agreement with the winner.

choices.text: The election had permanently ended fears about political conflict.
choices.feedback: The letter shows ongoing conflict, not the disappearance of fear.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. The evidence would support the idea that a party could lose office, accept the transfer, and remain an organized opposition.
questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. Focus on the combination of accepting defeat and continuing to organize.
walkthrough: Read the evidence for two actions: accept the transfer and continue opposition.
Ask which interpretation requires both facts rather than only one.
The disappearance-of-parties interpretation contradicts the letter.
The loser's-consent interpretation explains how conflict could continue inside the constitutional system.
This is a key Exam 2 habit: evidence can support a qualified interpretation rather than a simple story of harmony.

questions.hint: What does the letter accept, and what does it preserve?

questions.stem: A historian says an expedition through newly acquired territory proves government control. The expedition needed local interpreters, food, horses, permission, and knowledge. What should the historian do?

choices.text: Qualify the claim: the expedition extended knowledge and claims, but its dependence reveals incomplete control.
choices.feedback: This interpretation explains both the government's expanding reach and the expedition's reliance on Native worlds.

choices.text: Strengthen the claim because dependence on local help proves that sovereignty was already complete.
choices.feedback: Dependence on local communities points away from complete control.

choices.text: Abandon the subject because expeditions cannot reveal anything about sovereignty.
choices.feedback: The expedition is valuable evidence precisely because its dependence reveals the limits of state power.

choices.text: Conclude that gathering knowledge means the government had no interest in territorial expansion.
choices.feedback: The expedition's mapping, recording, and diplomatic purposes show the opposite.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. The strongest interpretation holds expansion and limitation together: the expedition increased state knowledge while exposing how much power remained outside U.S. control.
questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. Ask what the new evidence makes difficult for the original claim without erasing what the expedition did accomplish.
walkthrough: State the original claim: expedition equals already-established control.
List the new evidence of dependence on local communities.
That evidence is difficult to reconcile with complete sovereignty.
Do not swing to the opposite extreme: the expedition still expanded knowledge and diplomatic claims.
Qualify the interpretation so it explains both state ambition and state weakness.
questions.transferStrategy: Good historians revise the strength of a claim when new evidence shows both achievement and limitation.
questions.hint: Can the expedition show growing reach without proving complete control?

questions.stem: A government bans much foreign trade to avoid war, then expands customs surveillance and punishes smuggling. Which interpretation best applies Chapter 7's model of 'peaceable coercion'?

choices.text: Economic sanctions are automatically weaker than every military action.
choices.feedback: The question is not simply strength; it is how nonwar pressure changes state power at home.

choices.text: Avoiding foreign war can still require stronger government coercion at home.
choices.feedback: This is the lecture's central paradox of the Embargo.

questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. Focus on the relationship between the foreign-policy goal and the domestic means required to pursue it.

Identify the means: restrict trade and enforce those restrictions domestically.

questions.stem: A historian argues that the United States chose war in 1812 before seriously trying alternatives. Which evidence from the formal lecture most strongly weakens that interpretation?

choices.text: War Hawks became more influential in Congress and pressed for a military response to Britain.

choices.feedback: The divided vote shows controversy over war but does not by itself establish the sequence of alternatives.

choices.text: Tecumseh and Tenskwatawa pursued a movement that resisted further U.S. land expansion.
choices.feedback: This helps explain the western crisis but not whether the United States tried nonwar alternatives first.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. The sequence of diplomacy and economic coercion is direct evidence that war emerged after repeated alternatives rather than before them.
questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. Match the evidence to the exact claim being tested: whether serious alternatives came first.

Look for chronological evidence about policy before June 1812.

War Hawks and the divided vote matter to the broader story but do not test this particular claim as directly.
Choose the evidence that bears most directly on the claim.

questions.stem: A historian writes, 'Tecumseh's movement was simply a British creation.' Which new evidence would most strongly require the historian to qualify that claim?

choices.text: British officials sometimes supplied Native resistance movements with material and diplomatic support.
choices.feedback: That evidence fits the claim rather than requiring qualification.

choices.feedback: Suspicion helps explain American perceptions, but it does not prove how the movement actually originated or operated.

choices.text: Tecumseh and Tenskwatawa pursued their own religious, political, and anti-cession goals amid Native disagreement.
choices.feedback: This shows Indigenous agency and internal politics that cannot be reduced to British control.

choices.text: The United States and Britain later fought a war that also involved conflict in the West.
choices.feedback: That later war does not by itself establish the origins of Tecumseh's movement.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. British connections mattered, but independent Indigenous goals and internal Native politics require a more complex interpretation than 'British creation.'
questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. Look for evidence that is hardest to explain if the movement had no independent Indigenous purpose.
walkthrough: State the original interpretation: British agency explains the movement.
Ask what evidence would be difficult for that interpretation to absorb.
Independent religious and political goals point to Native agency, while disagreements among Native communities reveal internal politics.
British support can remain part of the explanation without becoming the entire explanation.
The revised interpretation should say British connections interacted with an Indigenous resistance project rather than creating it from nothing.
questions.transferStrategy: When a claim reduces one group to another group's instrument, look for evidence of independent goals, choices, and internal disagreement.
questions.hint: What evidence shows they were pursuing something Britain did not invent?

questions.stem: Which interpretation best connects the Whiskey Rebellion in Lecture 1 to the party crisis in Lecture 2?

choices.text: Once the government proved it could enforce laws, political opposition became unnecessary.
choices.feedback: The opposite occurred: stronger federal capacity intensified arguments over how that power might be used.

choices.text: New federal power raised the stakes of controlling government, helping turn disagreement into organized opposition.
choices.feedback: This explains how the achievement of Lecture 1 helped create the problem of Lecture 2.

choices.text: Building federal capacity solved the problem of legitimacy so completely that parties could develop without fear.
choices.feedback: The party crisis shows that legitimacy remained unsettled.

choices.text: The two lectures are unrelated because one concerns taxation and the other newspapers.
choices.feedback: The chapter is organized around how one form of power created the conditions for the next political problem.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. State-building increased the importance of who controlled the state, helping make organized opposition both more necessary and more frightening.
questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. Ask how solving the problem of weak government could create a new political problem.
walkthrough: Identify Lecture 1's outcome: the federal government gained real fiscal and coercive capacity.
Identify Lecture 2's problem: citizens organized to defeat the people controlling that power.
Ask how the first development changes the stakes of the second.
A stronger government gives political control more consequences, so opposition becomes more urgent and more alarming.
The strongest connection treats the lectures as a causal sequence rather than two separate topics.

questions.stem: Which connection best links Hamilton's Bank debate to Jefferson's Louisiana Purchase dilemma?

choices.text: Both show leaders using implied or practical power when the Constitution offered no simple operating instruction.
choices.feedback: This connects two different policies through the recurring problem of constitutional power in practice.

choices.text: Both prove Hamilton and Jefferson always agreed on constitutional interpretation.
choices.feedback: Their general constitutional instincts differed even though Jefferson later faced his own practical dilemma.

choices.text: Both concern exactly the same constitutional clause and therefore required the same legal answer.
choices.feedback: The connection is broader than a single clause: both involve governing beyond an explicit instruction manual.

choices.text: Both show that constitutional arguments mattered only when the government was weak.
choices.feedback: The arguments became especially important because the government was gaining the capacity to act.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. The connection is not that Hamilton and Jefferson became identical, but that governing repeatedly forced Americans to interpret powers the Constitution did not spell out in operational detail.
questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. Look for the recurring constitutional problem rather than identical policies or identical beliefs.
walkthrough: Identify the Bank problem: can legitimate ends justify implied means?
Identify the Purchase problem: can a president act when a major opportunity is not neatly covered by explicit text?
Compare them using the same criterion: how constitutional power works in practice.
The strongest connection preserves Hamilton and Jefferson's differences while showing that both faced the 'instruction manual' problem.
That makes the chapter's constitutional argument larger than either policy.
questions.transferStrategy: A strong connection can reveal a recurring problem even when historical actors answer it differently.
questions.hint: What problem do the Bank and the Purchase share even though the policies differ?

questions.stem: Which interpretation best connects the Louisiana Purchase to the western crisis that helped lead toward war in 1812?

choices.text: Political disagreement had disappeared by the Jefferson and Madison years.
choices.feedback: Both episodes show deep disagreement, not its disappearance.

choices.text: Every major national decision required unanimous consent from voters, representatives, and political parties.
choices.feedback: The war vote was sharply divided, and the election crisis did not produce unanimity.

choices.text: Partisan conflict mattered only during elections and not in foreign policy.
choices.feedback: The war vote shows partisan and sectional conflict over foreign policy as well.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. Chapter 7 suggests that constitutional durability did not require harmony; it required institutions capable of containing disagreement without treating every defeat as the end of the republic.
questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. Ask what both episodes reveal about disagreement rather than about consensus.
walkthrough: Identify the common feature: intense political disagreement.
Identify the institutional outcome in 1801: power transfers rather than the system collapsing.
Identify the institutional outcome in 1812: Congress makes a contested decision through voting.
Together they support an interpretation of republican durability through managed conflict, not unanimity.
This also qualifies any story that treats political stability as the absence of disagreement.
questions.transferStrategy: For synthesis, look for the institutional pattern that survives across different kinds of conflict.
questions.hint: What survived even when Americans sharply disagreed?

questions.stem: Which interpretation best captures the throughline of all four Chapter 7 lectures?

choices.text: The republic survived through more power, opposition, expansion, and war, while each solution reopened questions about liberty and legitimacy.
choices.feedback: This interpretation accounts for the distinct problem in each lecture and connects them into one developmental story.

choices.text: Completing the Revolution meant steadily reducing national power until government became almost invisible.
choices.feedback: The lectures show national capacity, partisan institutions, territorial claims, and war-making choices expanding rather than disappearing.

choices.text: The Revolution was completed once the Constitution was ratified, so later conflicts were separate from its unresolved questions.
choices.feedback: Chapter 7 treats those later conflicts as continuing arguments over the meaning of republican liberty and power.

choices.text: Every conflict after 1789 grew from a single disagreement between Hamilton and Jefferson over policy.
choices.feedback: Their conflict mattered, but the chapter includes Native sovereignty, institutional precedent, popular opposition, and war beyond that personal rivalry.

questions.conciseCorrectFeedback: Exactly. Chapter 7's larger story is not that the Revolution ended, but that Americans kept institutionalizing it through choices that expanded power and reopened the question of liberty.
questions.conciseIncorrectFeedback: Not quite. Look for the interpretation that can explain all four lectures without flattening them into one personality conflict or one direction of change.
walkthrough: Test the interpretation against Lecture 1: can it explain precedent and federal capacity?
Test it against Lecture 2: can it explain legitimate organized opposition?
Test it against Lecture 3: can it explain territorial expansion and contested sovereignty?
Test it against Lecture 4: can it explain why a republic suspicious of war eventually chose it?
The strongest chapter-level interpretation covers all four while preserving the new problem each solution created.
questions.transferStrategy: For synthesis, test a broad interpretation against every major case. If it fails one lecture, it is probably too narrow.
questions.hint: Which answer can survive evidence from all four lectures?
